rights_note: This starter desk contains two short passage units, not complete books. The English selections are older public-domain translations (Pope, Butler, Dryden and Mackail); source editions and credits are linked below. Ancient originals are credited to their digital text providers. No modern copyrighted translation is reproduced. Texts are aligned by passage, not word or translated line; typography is retained where practical. Provider terms and territorial copyright can differ for material beyond these selections.

passages.title: Iliad · the opening anger
passages.original:
μῆνιν ἄειδε θεὰ Πηληϊάδεω Ἀχιλῆος
οὐλομένην, ἣ μυρίʼ Ἀχαιοῖς ἄλγεʼ ἔθηκε,
πολλὰς δʼ ἰφθίμους ψυχὰς Ἄϊδι προΐαψεν
ἡρώων, αὐτοὺς δὲ ἑλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν
οἰωνοῖσί τε πᾶσι, Διὸς δʼ ἐτελείετο βουλή,
ἐξ οὗ δὴ τὰ πρῶτα διαστήτην ἐρίσαντε
Ἀτρεΐδης τε ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν καὶ δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς.
passages.original_credit: Homer; Monro/Allen text, Perseus Digital Library / Tufts University. Seven lines extracted from TEI; markup removed, wording retained. This Greek excerpt is offered under CC BY-SA 4.0, as in the provider repository; attribution does not imply endorsement.

translations.name: Samuel Butler · prose
translations.credit: Samuel Butler (1835–1902); Project Gutenberg eBook 2199. Public-domain translation; transcription credits on source page.
translations.text: Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles son of Peleus, that brought countless ills upon the Achaeans. Many a brave soul did it send hurrying down to Hades, and many a hero did it yield a prey to dogs and vultures, for so were the counsels of Jove fulfilled from the day on which the son of Atreus, king of men, and great Achilles, first fell out with one another.

translations.name: Alexander Pope · verse
translations.credit: Alexander Pope (1688–1744); Project Gutenberg eBook 6130. Eight English lines corresponding to the opening Greek passage. Public-domain translation; source notes not reproduced.
translations.text:
Achilles’ wrath, to Greece the direful spring
Of woes unnumber’d, heavenly goddess, sing!
That wrath which hurl’d to Pluto’s gloomy reign
The souls of mighty chiefs untimely slain;
Whose limbs unburied on the naked shore,
Devouring dogs and hungry vultures tore.
Since great Achilles and Atrides strove,
Such was the sovereign doom, and such the will of Jove!

prompts.question: Compare 'anger' and 'wrath'. What expectations does each create? Identify another difference in how the harm is described.
Compare the opening word order and the prose/verse rhythm. What changes when you read both aloud?
Identify one interpretive choice you can support from this passage and one question you would need Greek commentary to resolve.

passages.guidance: Both versions invoke a goddess and introduce Achilles' destructive anger, but the verse and prose organize the material differently. Distinguish your response to English style from claims about accuracy. A pleasing phrase alone cannot settle what the Greek permits; the English line counts are not the Greek line counts. These prompts have no automatic grade.

passages.title: Aeneid · war, exile and beginnings
passages.original:
Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs
Ītaliam fātō profugus Lāvīniaque vēnit
lītora, multum ille et terrīs iactātus et altō
vī superum, saevae memorem Iūnōnis ob īram,
multa quoque et bellō passus, dum conderet urbem
īnferretque deōs Latiō; genus unde Latīnum
Albānīque patrēs atque altae moenia Rōmae.
passages.original_credit: Virgil; Latin passage checked against Dickinson College Commentaries, edited by Christopher Francese and Meghan Reedy. Ancient text with displayed macrons retained; modern commentary is linked, not copied.

translations.name: John Dryden · verse
translations.credit: John Dryden (1631–1700); Internet Classics Archive at MIT. Ten English lines for the seven-line Latin unit. Public-domain translation.
translations.text:
Arms, and the man I sing, who, forc'd by fate,
And haughty Juno's unrelenting hate,
Expell'd and exil'd, left the Trojan shore.
Long labors, both by sea and land, he bore,
And in the doubtful war, before he won
The Latian realm, and built the destin'd town;
His banish'd gods restor'd to rites divine,
And settled sure succession in his line,
From whence the race of Alban fathers come,
And the long glories of majestic Rome.

translations.name: J. W. Mackail · prose
translations.credit: J. W. Mackail (1859–1945), 1885 translation; Project Gutenberg eBook 22456. Public-domain translation; source transcription credits retained at the linked page.
translations.text: I sing of arms and the man who of old from the coasts of Troy came, an exile of fate, to Italy and the shore of Lavinium; hard driven on land and on the deep by the violence of heaven, for cruel Juno's unforgetful anger, and hard bestead in war also, ere he might found a city and carry his gods into Latium; from whom is the Latin race, the lords of Alba, and the stately city Rome.

prompts.question: Track fate, exile and Juno in both versions. Which phrases change the emphasis or arrangement?
Compare the two versions' final references to Rome. How does verse or prose shape the sound and apparent grandeur?
Use the linked commentary to examine arma virumque. Separate what the source explains from your own proposed connection with Homer.

passages.guidance: The opening joins war, a traveller and Rome's projected origins. The Dickinson notes connect the first two Latin terms with the Iliad and Odyssey. Compare the translators' order and descriptive additions before making claims about fidelity. Pietas appears later in the opening (1.10), not in the seven lines displayed here.

glossary.title: Stoicism
glossary.body: A Hellenistic philosophical school with connected accounts of logic, nature and ethics. Its ethical emphasis on virtue and judgments is not simply a rule to suppress all emotion. Ancient authors and modern uses of 'stoic' should be distinguished.
glossary.task: Compare a claim by Epictetus with the ordinary modern meaning of 'stoic'.

glossary.title: Patronage · patronus / cliens
glossary.body: An unequal relationship of reciprocal support and obligation in Roman society. Assistance, advocacy and public loyalty could be involved; patronage of writers is one application, not the whole institution. Its arrangements changed across periods and settings.
glossary.task: Ask what a literary dedication shows about support, and what it cannot establish about a writer's independence.

glossary.title: Elegy & the elegiac couplet
glossary.body: In ancient Greek and Latin, elegiac poetry is associated with a metrical pair: a dactylic hexameter followed by a pentameter. Its subjects can include love, politics and commemoration. Do not assume every ancient elegy is a lament for the dead, as the modern English genre often is.
glossary.task: Identify form and subject separately when reading a translated elegy; an English translation may not retain the original meter.

glossary.title: Epic · narrative and invocation
glossary.body: For this desk, compare the extended narratives of Homer and Virgil and their openings addressing or invoking a divine source of song. The pairing is a starting point, not a definition covering every epic tradition. English verse and prose versions need not reproduce the original meter.
glossary.task: Compare the opening focus of the Iliad and Aeneid in the Reading desk.

reception.title: Antigone → Antigone
reception.body: The publisher explicitly connects Anouilh's play with Sophocles and discusses the ambiguity of its wartime political reception. The later play should not be reduced to a single unambiguous political message.
reception.task: Compare the two Creon–Antigone confrontations. What changes in the case made by each speaker?

reception.title: Metamorphoses → Pygmalion and Galatea
reception.to_title: Jean-Léon Gérôme · Pygmalion and Galatea, ca. 1890
reception.body: The Met identifies the painting's subject with the story in Ovid and describes Gérôme's multiple painted and sculpted versions. A depicted moment is not a full retelling, and the museum's object date is approximate.
reception.task: Open the museum image and compare its chosen moment with the episode. Whose viewpoint does the picture invite?

reception.title: Odyssey → the Coens' wandering musicians
reception.to_title: Inside Llewyn Davis / O Brother, Where Art Thou?
reception.body: Sight and Sound identifies explicit Odyssey references in these two films. This supports a trail of allusions, not a claim that either is a scene-for-scene translation or that Homer is their sole source.
reception.task: Track a named allusion and a looser resemblance. Which can you document, and which is your own reading? Use a legal viewing source; the reference is a review, not the films.

reception.title: Antigone ↔ A Doll's House
reception.body: An editorial pairing about duty, household and self-definition. No direct influence or adaptation is asserted, and this entry is not evidence of a historical transmission chain.
reception.task: Test the pairing against both endings. Identify a difference that makes the analogy less convincing.
